strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated by prior interpretability findings (Zhou et al., 2024) that LLMs internally learn Fourier-like features for numbers, and is backed by clean theoretical justification (Lemma 3.3/3.4) showing exact digit recoverability via modular arithmetic on circular embeddings.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple arithmetic tasks (addition, subtraction, multiplication, decimal arithmetic, modular arithmetic, binary classification) with strong and consistent results: FoNE is the only method achieving 100% accuracy on over 100K test examples across several tasks, with substantial data efficiency (64x less data) and parameter efficiency gains over subword/digit-wise tokenization and xVal.

Thorough ablation studies (choice of periods, necessity of sine/cosine vs. direct digit encoding, linear projection vs. zero padding) that support the design choices with concrete failure-mode analysis (e.g., mod5 confusing digits 2 and 7).

Demonstrates scalability beyond the main synthetic benchmarks: 60-digit addition via chunking, combination with Abacus positional embeddings for length generalization, and comparison against a more recent competitive baseline (Number Token Loss), where FoNE substantially outperforms all NTL variants.

Provides evidence that FoNE does not harm (and can even improve) general language modeling ability via GPT-2 pretraining on FineWeb and continual pretraining of Llama-3.1-1B, addressing a natural concern about integrating a specialized numerical embedding into general-purpose LMs.

Good engineering detail and reproducibility: explicit algorithms in the appendix, discussion of practical integration (numeric parsers, [NUM] token), and a discussion section addressing several natural design questions (why classification loss, why base 10, why FoNE outperforms other embeddings).
weaknesses: The primary empirical validation remains on synthetic, controlled arithmetic tasks with small operand ranges (up to 6 digits) and small-to-medium models trained from scratch; there is limited evidence of benefit on realistic downstream numerical reasoning tasks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, real quantitative reasoning benchmarks) beyond a narrow arithmetic slice of Brown et al. (2020) and MMLU (which shows no meaningful improvement, only no degradation).

The continual pretraining experiment uses a 'simplified' version of FoNE that differs substantially from the full proposed method (building on top of BPE tokens and learning only a projection layer rather than overriding embeddings and the special [NUM] token/decoding scheme), suggesting the full method may be difficult to integrate into existing pretrained LLMs and undermining claims of general applicability to LLM pretraining.

The decoding mechanism requires a special [NUM] token and a bespoke digit-wise classification head, which is a nontrivial architectural change to standard LM generation/decoding and is not evaluated in the more realistic pretraining-from-scratch-on-FineWeb setting for actual arithmetic performance (only perplexity is reported there, not arithmetic accuracy or generation quality on numeric outputs).

The method has intrinsic limitations for large numbers (float64 precision ceiling requiring chunking into 5-digit groups), and the effectiveness of this chunking heuristic is only demonstrated on one synthetic 60-digit addition setting rather than more diverse or naturally occurring long-number scenarios.

The core novelty is largely in directly operationalizing an already-known interpretability insight (Fourier features naturally emerge in pretrained LLMs) rather than a fundamentally new representational idea; the technical contribution is incremental relative to Zhou et al. (2024) and related sinusoidal/DICE/SALSA works, mainly differing in choosing digit-aligned base-10 periods and a parallel decoding scheme.

Some baseline comparisons could be strengthened - e.g., limited justification that hyperparameters (learning rates, epochs) for digit-wise/subword/xVal/NTL baselines were tuned as extensively as FoNE, and the WikiTableQuestions token-efficiency claim is a single anecdotal statistic rather than a broader real-world task evaluation.
